title: Rights Groups Say NRI Fans Face a 'Climate of Fear' at the World Cup. FIFA Has Not Responded.
excerpt: With the tournament kicking off June 11 across the United States, the Sport and Rights Alliance warns that Trump's immigration crackdown has turned the world's biggest sporting event into a source of anxiety for diaspora fans and travellers on temporary visas.
body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup starts next Wednesday. Forty-eight teams. Sixteen cities. Eleven stadiums across the United States, plus venues in Canada and Mexico. For millions of Indian-origin fans living in North America, this was supposed to be the biggest football event in their time zone, ever.

Instead, it arrives shadowed by something unprecedented for a World Cup: an immigration crackdown by the host nation's government, and a formal warning from international rights groups that FIFA has failed to protect fans.

## "A Distinctively Dangerous Climate of Fear"

On Wednesday, the Sport & Rights Alliance — a coalition of human rights organisations that monitors major sporting events — issued a public statement accusing FIFA of allowing a "distinctively dangerous climate of fear" to develop around the tournament.

"FIFA's weak response to the human rights threats documented by local groups and global civil society organisations means that we are witnessing a distinctively dangerous climate of fear, uncertainty, and repression," said Andrea Florence, the coalition's executive director.

The group cited visa restrictions, border enforcement, and policing as specific concerns, particularly for fans travelling on temporary visas — a category that includes millions of Indian nationals in the US on H-1B, L-1, and student visas, as well as undocumented diaspora residents.

## What This Means for NRI Fans

India does not have a team in the World Cup. But the Indian diaspora in the United States is enormous — more than 4.8 million people of Indian origin, the largest immigrant group in the country. Cities hosting World Cup matches — New York, Dallas, Houston, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Seattle — are precisely the metros with the highest concentrations of Indian-American residents.

Many NRI fans will attend as neutrals, drawn to matches featuring the sport's biggest stars. Others will support Qatar, whose squad includes 19-year-old Tahsin Mohammed — born to Keralite parents from Thalassery and Valapattanam, and the tournament's most prominent player of Indian heritage.

But the warning from the Sport & Rights Alliance specifically highlights what could happen at or around stadiums. The Trump administration's mass deportation raids, aggressive enforcement at transportation hubs, and the broader chilling effect on communities with mixed immigration status have created uncertainty that goes beyond usual World Cup logistics.

## "The Safest and Most Secure in History"

The White House pushed back. Spokesman Davis Ingle said President Trump "is focused on ensuring that this is not only an incredible experience for all fans and visitors, but also the safest and most secure in history." He dismissed the concerns as "ridiculous scare tactics driven by liberal activist groups and the left-wing media."

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino has repeatedly promised that the world will be welcomed to the United States. But FIFA did not immediately respond to the Sport & Rights Alliance statement.

## The Broadcast Saga Adds Context

For NRI fans who choose to stay home, the picture has only recently cleared. Until last week, India was one of the last major markets without a confirmed World Cup broadcaster — an extraordinary situation for a country of 1.4 billion people. Zee Entertainment finally secured the rights on May 29, just 13 days before kickoff, after months of failed negotiations and a Delhi High Court petition demanding free-to-air coverage on Doordarshan.

Meanwhile, a Washington DC-based Indian-American investment firm, Avni LLC, had publicly claimed to have submitted a $300 million corporate guarantee in FIFA's closed tender process for the Indian subcontinent. Whether that bid played a role in forcing Zee's hand remains unclear. FIFA said only that discussions "are ongoing and must remain confidential."

The broadcast will air on Zee's Unite8 Sports channels and stream on ZEE5. But the scramble — and the fact that Indian fans came within days of a total blackout — underlined how far football's governing body is from treating the Indian market with the seriousness cricket's governing bodies learned long ago.

## Four Players, No Team

India itself is absent. The country has never qualified for a FIFA World Cup, a fact that stings harder every four years. But the 2026 edition will feature at least four players of Indian heritage — Tahsin Mohammed (Qatar), Sarpreet Singh (New Zealand), and others — none of whom wear India's blue.

For NRI fans, the tournament was always going to be bittersweet. Now, it arrives with a layer of unease that has nothing to do with football and everything to do with what it means to be a diaspora community in today's America.

The first match kicks off June 11 in Mexico City. Mexico plays South Africa. India's fans will be watching — from living rooms, sports bars, and, for some, stadiums where they have been told to carry their passports.

*Sources: Reuters, Sport & Rights Alliance statement (June 3, 2026), The Indian EYE, Khel Now, USA Today*
